strengths: The position-wise reciprocal loss model is an interpretable empirical contribution relevant to understanding language-model pretraining. The reported R² > 0.95 for over 99% of checkpoints, including evaluation on Pile and PG-19, provides encouraging evidence for this regularity within the studied setting.

The experimental investment is substantial: two model sizes trained for 400B tokens, checkpoints every 1B tokens, and evaluations on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution text. Figure 1 reports consistently lower forecasting errors than the supplied baselines across multiple observation budgets.

The paper provides explicit forecasting equations and boundary conditions, and complements curve fitting with position-weighting interventions across eight downstream benchmarks. These experiments support the narrower, useful observation that uniform weighting remains competitive with the three tested alternatives.
weaknesses: The forecasting evaluation does not adequately separate discovering the law from testing it. Section 3.3 selects the functional forms and transition point using complete training trajectories, while Section 3.4 evaluates prefix-based forecasts on those same trajectories. Although forecast coefficients use early observations, future behavior has informed model selection. Separate discovery and evaluation runs, with the functional form and transition rule fixed beforehand, are needed to establish predictive reliability. This unresolved validation issue is a principal reason for recommending resubmission next cycle.

The baselines do not isolate the contribution of token-position modeling. The proposed predictor incorporates the known cosine learning-rate schedule, whereas the comparison functions do not. After the transition, Equation 10 reduces to a constant plus a2 because a0 and a1 are fixed. A crucial missing ablation therefore fits the same piecewise, schedule-aware function directly to aggregate loss. The power-law baseline also needs an explicit specification, including whether it has an asymptotic loss floor; calling it 'Exponential' in Figure 1 makes the comparison ambiguous.

The evidence supports a substantially narrower scope than a general temporal scaling law for LLMs. Both sizes use one architecture family, tokenizer, training corpus, training horizon, and cosine schedule, with evaluation at a single context length. PG-19 changes the evaluation distribution but does not test a different training recipe. Sensitivity to the transition point and validation on an unseen training horizon or schedule would materially strengthen the claim. Applications to hyperparameter selection, data-mixture optimization, and early stopping remain prospective.

The uniform-learning interpretation exceeds the evidence. Equation 16 follows directly from imposing constant a0 and a1; Figure 4 adds evidence of approximately similar, smoothed loss reductions, but equal loss reduction does not establish equal optimization dynamics or imply that reweighting cannot help. Three suppression strategies introduced only after 100B tokens, without reported run variability or equivalence analysis, cannot establish the general unnecessaryness of position weighting. Table 2 supports competitiveness among these tested configurations.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Section 3.3 refers to an appendix of fitted parameters that is absent from the supplied manuscript. The nonlinear fitting procedure, initialization and parameter constraints, global batch size needed to translate warmup steps into tokens, and downstream evaluation implementation are insufficiently specified. The transition point is also inconsistent: 40% of 400B tokens implies 160B, whereas Section 4.1 states 120B. These omissions directly affect reproducing the headline forecasting results.

The novelty framing mischaracterizes prior work. Kaplan et al. (2020) already investigates training curves and dependence on training steps, so the repeated assertion that temporal training behavior was previously untouched is inaccurate. The contribution should be positioned around the particular positional decomposition and schedule-dependent forecasting construction, with comparisons to existing learning-curve models.

Equation 5 is not a valid general probabilistic justification: having more context does not imply that the probability of a different next token exceeds that of the preceding token. An appropriate information-theoretic statement concerns conditional entropy in expectation under stated assumptions, and would still not derive the proposed reciprocal form. The reciprocal relationship should be presented as an empirical finding rather than as following from this inequality.
